Nov 21 : Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, rose more than 8 per cent to around $59,952 on Saturday, after sliding to its lowest level in two years earlier in the day.  It briefly crossed $60,000 at around 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).  Bitcoin had fallen to $55,251.60 earlier in the day, its lowest level in two years, after breaking below $57,742 on Friday for the first time since September 2024 as stretched valuations in artificial intelligence stocks rattled investors and weighed on other risk assets.  Crypto markets have been shaken in recent sessions by weeks of concern about the profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks following Democrats' win in the US midterm elections and the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic's momentous market debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally.

Nov 20 : SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible trillion-dollar "buyout" of South Korean memory chip company SK Hynix, the Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The Information quoted a SoftBank spokesperson as saying Son was no longer considering such a deal.  “SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration,” the report said, citing the spokesperson.  SK Hynix said in a statement it has no knowledge of the matter described in the Information report. It added that any foreign acquisition of the company would require prior government approval under Korean law. A SoftBank spokesperson referred to the statement the company gave to the Information, when Reuters sought a comment.

Source: Reuters

SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on Saturday (Nov 21) urged the country to move fast as it competes in the global artificial intelligence (AI) race, as he toured a data centre under construction in the southeastern city of Ulsan. "The whole world is competing right now, and speed is vital," Lee said in a public video of his tour. Data centres are a major source of chip demand, and he hoped the success of the project, built by South Korea's second-largest conglomerate SK Group, would draw further investment from global AI companies, Lee said. SK Group is developing the Ulsan data centre jointly with Amazon Web Services (AWS). The estimated cost is 7 trillion won (US$5.2 billion) until 2029, South Korea's science ministry said last year. Operations are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2027. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won said in September that the capacity under construction was an initial 103 megawatt by 2029, with plans to expand it by nearly 900 megawatts in the future. The group is also planning further partnerships with global technology companies as the project progresses, Chey said. On Saturday, President Lee said AI investment had mainly been concentrated around Seoul, and that the Ulsan project showed regional growth was possible. After being told that about 900 people were working at the site, Lee said advanced facilities were short of construction workers and that ministries needed to consider how to train the workforce for building data centres and AI infrastructure.

Source: Reuters/as

Nov 20 : GTCR is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments, the private equity group said in a filing on Friday, days after reports that a consortium effort with CD&R was dropped. Shares of Global Payments closed the day 10 per cent higher. It was up about 19 per cent so far in 2026. GTCR is working with other private equity firms to finance the potential deal, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. GTCR, which holds a 16.35 per cent stake in Global Payments and is the largest shareholder, said no definitive decision has been made. Global Payments did not immediately respond to Reuters request for a comment.

Private equity firms CD&R and GTCR had dropped their pursuit of Global Payments as a buyout consortium, Reuters reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter. The report had added that it was possible that CD&R and GTCR will resume the talks with Global Payments at a later date or another buyer for the company may emerge. Atlanta-based Global Payments is one of the world's largest payment processors. It enables merchants to accept card and digital payments and provides software and technology services to businesses. Its market value stood at about $22 billion, as of last close. The company has faced pressure in recent years from slowing growth in some business lines, intensifying competition and investor demands to boost profitability. Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover deal first and said it could value Global Payments at $50 billion, including debt and premium.

Nov 20 : Hackers this week breached a system that the US Department of Agriculture uses to send payments to farmers, NBC News reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter. The department notified employees of the incident on Thursday, the former officials told NBC. While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. It is not known who was responsible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the USDA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nov 20 : CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire rival cybersecurity provider Zscaler amid consolidation in the security software sector, according to two people familiar with the matter. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, the sources said. No deal is guaranteed, and the discussions could still end without an agreement, the people added. Shares of Zscaler, which has a market capitalization of about $32 billion as of Friday's close, jumped 17 per cent in after-hours trading. CrowdStrike shares fell 8 per cent. A combination would create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers as enterprise customers seek to reduce the number of security vendors they use, favoring providers that can deliver multiple products through a single relationship.

CrowdStrike and Zscaler did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform is widely used to secure endpoints such as laptops, servers and mobile devices, while Zscaler specializes in cloud-based network security services that help companies securely connect users to applications without relying on traditional corporate networks. Founded in 2011 by chief executive George Kurtz, CrowdStrike has grown into one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, helping organizations detect and respond to cyber threats through its cloud-native software platform. The Austin, Texas-based company has expanded beyond endpoint protection through acquisitions and internal development into areas including cloud, identity and threat intelligence security. The deal would address one of CrowdStrike's biggest gaps in network security and help it compete more directly with platform providers such as Palo Alto Networks. Zscaler, founded in 2007 by chief executive Jay Chaudhry, pioneered zero-trust security, which continuously verifies users and devices before granting access to corporate applications and data. Its cloud-based software lets employees securely access applications from any location. Any transaction would likely require the backing of Chaudhry, who remains Zscaler's largest shareholder. The discussions come as cybersecurity companies race to expand offerings to meet demand for integrated platforms that address a wider range of threats. Zscaler's shares fell sharply earlier this year in a broader software selloff as investors weighed the impact of artificial intelligence, but have since rebounded. Bloomberg News first reported on the merger discussion.

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : Coding startup Cognition AI is in funding talks at a $75 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The company is considering raising $2 billion or more in the latest round, the report said, adding that the talks were ongoing and the details could change. The news comes about two months after Cognition raised $2 billion in a Series E funding round at a valuation of $48 billion. The round was led by new investors Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, alongside existing backers Founders Fund, General Catalyst, and Avenir. Cognition did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The company is an AI startup that develops autonomous software-engineering agents, which can plan, write, test and deploy code with limited human intervention. The company was valued at $26 billion in a funding round in May, when it raised $1 billion.

Nov 20 : The US Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday proposed taking direct control of a comprehensive industry-funded market surveillance tool long the subject of cost and privacy complaints, the agency announced. The proposal makes good on the Trump administration's pledge to rework the so-called Consolidated Audit Trail, which the agency first mandated following the 2010 "flash crash," in which Wall Street indices temporarily erased nearly $1 trillion in market value in minutes. The surveillance system remains the only source of its kind for comprehensive, real-time data and information about market events — allowing regulators to reconstruct every order, route and execution for US-listed equities and options nationwide — making it crucial to investigations into possible market misconduct including insider trading and market manipulation. But investment industry and stock market operators have battled over who should foot the bill for its development and operations costs while conservative critics earlier decried what they said was the CAT's invasive collection of personal data.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in Friday's statement the changes would make the CAT "accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs," to the benefit of both exchange operators and market participants. But under Friday's proposal, stock exchanges and broker-dealers themselves would collect and report the same data to the agency or its designee, giving the SEC direct control, the agency said. The new rules would also subject the system's costs to annual funding legislation from Congress, something market operators and others warn could expose it to government shutdowns. WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Honda and Toyota Motor said on Friday they are recalling about 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs over a risk that Takata airbag inflators could rupture. Honda and Toyota both said there were no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no airbag inflator ruptures. The automakers will replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles. There have, however, been at least 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009, an issue prompting the largest auto recall in US history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a drying agent. At least 20 of those deaths were in Honda vehicles. The vehicles in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks. "Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA said late Friday, adding that other automakers continue to conduct inflator analysis and testing. The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the United States. The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 IS250, 2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles. The Honda recall covers vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity and large temperature fluctuations. Over the past decade, two dozen major automakers have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators worldwide, including about 67 million vehicles in the United States. Various automakers have also reported hundreds of injuries in vehicles since 2009 from Takata airbag inflators that can explode, unleashing metal shrapnel inside cars and trucks, killing or injuring drivers or other vehicle occupants. Honda said long-term monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions. Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries. The Honda recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in Alabama, California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands (Saipan), Guam and American Samoa. Toyota did not specify in which US states the recall applies but said it expects the replacement inflators will be ready by early 2027.

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Alphabet's self-driving unit Waymo said on Friday it is issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Earlier this week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on US freeways, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state. The California ban, which took effect last week, is a result of a series of incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said. Waymo said a statement it filed two safety recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Thursday on its automated driving system "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control."

The closed freeway lanes recall stems from unusual circumstances where a Waymo vehicle may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane, the company said, adding it is still working on the recall remedy. The manual traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6. Waymo says its technology outperforms statistically comparable human benchmarks and drastically reduces injury-causing crashes. Last week, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of its robotaxis passing stopped school buses. The probe will look into nearly 3,000 company-owned self-driving vehicles. Investigators want to determine whether a software update Waymo rolled out late last year failed to stop its driverless cars from passing school buses with flashing red lights. Most of the violations happened after the company said the remedy had been deployed. Nov 20 : Ford, Honda, Stellantis' FCA unit and Volkswagen sued New Jersey on Friday to block a new state law they say increases the amounts automakers must pay franchised dealers for warranty and recall repairs. In a complaint filed in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey, the automakers said the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives dealers a "blank check" to set prices for warranty, recall and other repair services, while prohibiting manufacturers from avoiding "extortionate" results or recovering the costs. New Jersey's law will shift more than $375 million a year to dealers from automakers, giving dealers a "windfall" by imposing no obligation to use the money to improve customer service or boost compensation for employees, the automakers said. "In short, the act rewards dealers for charging their customers more," the automakers said.

The office of New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, who enforces the state's laws, declined to comment. New Jersey's law took effect on April 1, after former Governor Phil Murphy signed it in September 2025. CONSTITUTIONAL VIOLATIONS ALLEGED The automakers objected to letting dealers charge a "labor multiplier" based on samples of repair orders, saying it lets dealers bill for substantially more labor time than they actually work. They also challenged provisions requiring automakers to pay marked-up prices on parts that the dealers received at reduced cost or for free, and preventing automakers from providing less expensive parts even if supply, demand or other factors justified price cuts. Ford, Honda, FCA — which includes Fiat and Chrysler — and Volkswagen said that since the law took effect, each has received dozens of bills requiring payment "for hours that no technician works, that surpass what comparable dealers charge for the same work, and that exceed what retail customers pay." They said the law violates the US Constitution's Commerce Clause and Takings Clause, is preempted by federal law governing recalls, and violates New Jersey's Constitution. The nonprofit advocacy group New Jersey Coalition of Automotive Retailers is also a defendant. Its president Laura Perrotta said she was confident the group would prevail. She accused automakers of having for decades "helped themselves" to deep discounts on parts and labor at dealers' expense, and said it is "not an option" for dealers competing for business to pass warranty and recall repair costs to consumers.

Source: Reuters

The deal also includes product safeguards for teens and is contingent on a majority of districts signing on, with finalization likely to take a few months, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter. Robinhood worked with Tesla to create a way for retail investors to cast their ballots automatically that won approval from the US Securities and Exchange Commission in September. Backers say such retail-voting plans will increase retail investors' voting participation rates, even as the SEC takes steps that could eliminate shareholder proposals at corporate meetings. Critics say Tesla and others like ExxonMobil are designing their programs to unfairly channel votes in favor of management recommendations. A shareholder resolution filed with Robinhood for its next annual meeting, seen by Reuters, could spark debate about the role of investor rights. In the resolution the activist group As You Sow says Robinhood limits customers to using its own voting platform that requires a "painstaking and time-consuming challenge" to vote on individual corporate ballot items, rather than using third-party voting services.

It also notes Robinhood's work with Tesla's management-friendly voting option. The limited voting choices create legal and reputational risks, said As You Sow in its resolution, which calls for Robinhood to review offering clients more ways to vote, "including an independent voting service of their choice." As You Sow leaders said ideally Robinhood might offer something like Vanguard's voting program which casts prorated shares of funds' votes according to investors' preferences. Vanguard clients can select among voting policies like one that tends to support environmental and social shareholder resolutions, or one that supports management recommendations. Robinhood "shouldn't be limiting choices," said Danielle Fugere, As You Sow president, in an interview. "You should get to choose. That's what voting is all about." Robinhood representatives did not respond to messages seeking comment.
